strengths: Introduces a fully discrete VQ-based EEG tokenizer that transforms single-channel signals into discrete token sequences, aligning EEG analysis with NLP-style tokenization and reducing model complexity.
Jointly models temporal patches and STFT spectral windows with frequency-band and temporal masking, directly addressing frequency representation collapse and capturing time-frequency motifs.
Evaluates on four EEG datasets (TUEV, TUAB, IIIC, CHB-MIT) and reports consistent improvements over strong baselines such as BIOT and LaBraM while using fewer parameters.
Comprehensive experiments include ablations over raw-only, STFT-only, and joint variants, as well as masking strategy, positional encoding, and vocabulary-size studies.
Provides token-level analyses (utilization, class-token uniqueness, retrieval, spectral entropy, visualization) that support the interpretability and class-distinctiveness of learned tokens.
The single-channel tokenization design is channel-agnostic and is shown to enhance an existing foundation model (LaBraM) when its neural tokenizer is replaced.
The method is generally well described, with public datasets and sufficient implementation details in the appendix for reproducing the main pipeline.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the framework combines existing components such as VQ-VAE, STFT, masked modeling, and linear attention with domain-specific adaptations rather than introducing fundamentally new learning principles.
The single-dataset pretraining setting limits the claimed foundation-model scalability; no cross-dataset or cross-channel-configuration evaluation is provided to substantiate broad generalization.
The spectral entropy analysis appears to apply DFT to discrete token indices, which is questionable because token IDs are categorical and arbitrary; this weakens the frequency-learning conclusions.
Statistical significance is not established; several improvements over baselines are within one standard deviation, and no significance tests or confidence intervals are reported.
No code or reproducibility artifact is mentioned, despite extensive hyperparameters; this hinders reproducibility for a top-tier venue.
Baseline comparison is limited to BIOT and LaBraM; other relevant EEG tokenization or foundation models such as BRANT, MMM, and DeWave are not empirically compared.
Token uniqueness scores remain low (e.g., around 2% geometric mean), and interpretability evidence is largely qualitative and visual without expert validation.
Scalability claims are not supported by computational cost, latency, or cross-configuration experiments, and the downstream encoder still relies on multi-channel aggregation with channel embeddings.
Writing quality has multiple typos and citation errors (e.g., “Scable”, “Frequency Making Prediction”, misattributed VQ-VAE/GELU references), which reduce clarity.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: scalable, channel-agnostic EEG representation learning and discretization.
The proposed TFM-Tokenizer sensibly combines raw temporal patches with STFT-based frequency patches, vector quantization, and frequency/temporal masking.
Experiments span four EEG datasets and include several ablations and token-quality analyses, which is more than many papers in this space.
Reports parameter-efficient performance and shows that replacing LaBraM's neural tokenizer with TFM-Tokenizer can improve LaBraM on some metrics.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: discrete VQ tokenization, time-frequency modeling, and masked prediction are all well established; the contribution is largely an incremental combination for EEG. No fundamental methodological advance is demonstrated.

Claims are substantially stronger than the evidence. The paper repeatedly claims 'state-of-the-art', 'foundation model'-like scalability, and broad generalization, but all experiments use single-dataset pretraining and fixed 16-channel montages. There is no cross-dataset or cross-channel transfer study to support the central scalability claims.

The empirical gains are modest and often within variance. On TUEV, TFM-Token's balanced accuracy and kappa overlap with LaBraM's large standard deviations; on TUAB, CHB-MIT, and IIIC the improvement over the strongest baselines is small and lacks statistical significance testing.

The evaluation does not convincingly establish that the tokenizer is superior. Several baselines may not be ideally tuned in the single-dataset setting, and the paper does not compare against important VQ-based EEG tokenizers such as DeWave or other time-series tokenization methods adapted to EEG.

Token-quality metrics are ad hoc and not clearly meaningful. 'Class-Token Uniqueness' values are extremely low in absolute terms, and lower token utilization is treated as better without sufficient justification; codebook collapse or underuse could produce similar outcomes.

Interpretability evidence is qualitative and anecdotal. Visual inspection of selected tokens and classes does not establish systematic neurophysiological validity; there is no expert evaluation, quantitative motif analysis, or rigorous failure-case assessment.

Technical presentation and notation contain errors and inconsistencies: e.g., the STFT equation, the tokenizer function notation R^T -> V^{N x D}, and the use of ⊙/⊘ for element-wise multiplication. Citations are also misattributed in places (e.g., GELU, VQ-VAE, BERT).

Reproducibility and clinical impact are insufficiently addressed. No code/data release is mentioned, hyperparameter tuning details are partial, and there is no discussion of clinical deployment risks, dataset bias, or privacy/ethical considerations for EEG health applications.

strengths: Introduces a fully discrete EEG tokenization framework based on VQ-VAE with joint time-frequency modeling, addressing limitations of continuous embeddings and multi-channel dependence.

The TFM-Tokenizer is well-designed, combining a localized spectral window encoder, temporal encoder, frequency/temporal masking, and codebook quantization; the TFM-Encoder uses masked token prediction and linear attention for downstream tasks.
Extensive experiments on four EEG datasets (TUEV, TUAB, IIIC Seizure, CHB-MIT) against competitive baselines such as BIOT and LaBraM show consistent improvements and parameter efficiency.

Provides useful token-quality analyses, including token utilization, class-token uniqueness, similar-class retrieval, and spectral entropy, and demonstrates that the tokenizer can improve an existing foundation model (LaBraM).
Includes ablations on masking strategies, positional embeddings, vocabulary size, and single-domain tokenizer variants, supporting key design choices.
The appendix provides substantial implementation details, hyperparameters, and preprocessing information, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim of single-channel scalability is not directly evaluated on genuinely low-channel downstream tasks such as sleep staging; most main experiments use 16-channel montages or multi-channel settings, so cross-channel-configuration generalization remains unproven.
Evaluation is performed only in a single-dataset setting, with no cross-dataset or cross-task transfer experiments, despite the paper's motivation around foundation-model generalization.

There is a potential information-leakage issue in tokenizer pretraining: the raw EEG patch is provided unmasked while the model reconstructs a masked STFT, and the raw patch contains sufficient information to reconstruct the spectrogram, which may weaken the frequency-masking objective.

Some token-quality and frequency-learning metrics are ad hoc and not strongly validated; for example, class-token uniqueness and spectral entropy lack comparison to established measures, and the frequency-vs-temporal encoder analysis is not fully clear.

Component-level ablations for the Localized Spectral Window Encoder (e.g., frequency transformer, gated aggregation) are missing, and computational cost is not reported despite claims of parameter efficiency.

Baseline comparisons may not fully reflect the original models' pretraining regimes, and the absolute gains on TUEV/TUAB are modest; some percentage improvements are described in relative terms that can overstate the practical effect.

There is no discussion of ethical, privacy, or clinical-deployment concerns for EEG data, and minor notation/clarity issues (e.g., $M\oslash S$ for element-wise multiplication, typos such as 'Frequency Making') reduce readability.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: learning a reusable discrete token vocabulary for EEG signals, rather than only using tokenizers as auxiliary pretraining objectives.

The proposed TFM-Tokenizer is technically plausible and well motivated: it combines single-channel tokenization, dual-path time-frequency encoding, localized spectral windows, temporal encoding, VQ codebook learning, and joint frequency-temporal masking.

The single-channel design is a meaningful practical contribution: it enables channel-agnostic tokenization, flexible multi-channel aggregation, and cross-device scalability, as demonstrated on ear-EEG sleep staging.

The empirical evaluation is broad: four EEG benchmarks, single- and multi-dataset pretraining, comparisons against BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, NeuroLM, and multiple classic baselines, plus integration experiments with existing foundation models.

The paper provides substantial ablation and analysis, including frequency/temporal encoder variants, masking strategies, vocabulary size, positional encoding, downstream model size, token utilization, token uniqueness, consistency, and qualitative motif examples.
Reproducibility is relatively strong: code and pretrained weights are promised, and the appendix contains detailed preprocessing, dataset splits, hyperparameters, and implementation settings.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than high: the method largely combines existing ideas such as STFT-based time-frequency features, VQ-VAE-style codebooks, masked modeling, and transformer encoders. The core contribution is an EEG-specific adaptation rather than a fundamentally new tokenization principle.

Some claims are stronger than the evidence. The paper states that TFM-Tokenizer consistently outperforms all baselines in both settings, but on CHB-MIT with multi-dataset pretraining its balanced accuracy is lower than BIOT's, and performance is mixed across some metrics.

Baseline fairness is not fully resolved. LaBraM and BIOT are reproduced under smaller/constrained pretraining settings, while the original LaBraM and BIOT benefit from larger corpora. The paper acknowledges this but still uses these comparisons to support strong claims.

The downstream model ablation is not fully consistent with the final configuration: a 2-layer transformer appears to outperform the 4-layer model used in the main experiments on TUEV, raising questions about hyperparameter selection and whether the reported configuration is optimal.

Token-quality analyses are interesting but not entirely convincing in absolute terms. Class-token uniqueness scores remain very low, and the qualitative motif analysis is small-scale, so interpretability claims should be tempered.

The paper does not deeply analyze failure modes or robustness beyond a few settings. The fixed-window tokenization limitation is acknowledged, but its impact on clinical EEG events and long-duration patterns is not systematically studied.

strengths: The paper tackles a relevant problem: EEG tokenization for foundation models, with a clear motivation that existing EEG models often use continuous segment embeddings rather than reusable discrete vocabularies.
The proposed TFM-Tokenizer is reasonably well motivated: single-channel tokenization supports flexible multi-channel adaptation and potentially cross-device generalization.

The dual-path time-frequency design with localized spectral windows, temporal encoding, and joint frequency-temporal masking is technically plausible and represents a sensible combination of ideas from time-series and EEG representation learning.

The empirical study is broad: it evaluates on TUEV, TUAB, IIIC-Seizure, CHB-MIT, and an ear-EEG sleep staging dataset, and includes ablations on masking, token vocabulary, downstream depth, and token quality.
The paper demonstrates that the tokenizer can be plugged into existing models such as BIOT and LaBraM, sometimes improving their performance, which is a useful practical direction.
The authors provide substantial implementation details, hyperparameters, and a reproducibility statement with code availability, improving transparency.
The token analysis, including class-token uniqueness, consistency, and qualitative motif visualization, is a good step toward interpretability, even if the results are preliminary.
weaknesses: Novelty is overstated and incremental. The paper claims to be the first to learn a discrete EEG token vocabulary, but VQ-based neural tokenization for EEG already exists in LaBraM, and the main difference here is using the learned vocabulary as input rather than only as a pretraining target. The combination of VQ-VAE, STFT, dual-path encoding, and masked prediction is not sufficiently novel for a top-tier AI conference without stronger technical or empirical advances.

The evaluation is not fully convincing. Several improvements are small or within variance, and the method is not consistently best across datasets and metrics. For example, on CHB-MIT under multi-dataset pretraining, TFM-Tokenizer has lower balanced accuracy than BIOT, and many gains over reproduced baselines depend on the authors' reduced-data reproduction of LaBraM, which may not be a fair reference to the original model.

Baseline comparisons are questionable in places. LaBraM is reproduced using only four datasets and a much smaller pretraining corpus than the original, so comparisons labeled as LaBraM† may not reflect the true baseline strength. BIOT* and LaBraM* are also modified across settings, making it hard to separate tokenizer gains from experimental protocol differences.

The downstream model ablation undermines the proposed design choices. Table 11 shows that a 2-layer downstream transformer achieves higher Cohen's Kappa than the 4-layer model used in the main experiments, suggesting that the selected architecture may be suboptimal and that the reported performance could be improved or changed by better tuning.

Token quality evidence is weak in absolute terms. The class-token uniqueness scores are extremely small (e.g., 2.14% for TFM-Tokenizer on TUEV), and the retrieval/consistency results are moderate. The qualitative motif analysis only shows a few examples from two classes, so the interpretability claim is not strongly supported.

The scalability claim is based on a single ear-EEG sleep staging dataset with modest gains and only two foundation-model baselines. It does not rigorously establish device-agnostic generalization across broader non-standard EEG devices or signal types.

Technical clarity and writing need improvement. There are multiple typos and confusing statements (e.g., 'Taxens', 'Abnoral', inconsistent notation such as E_i^T/E_i^F, and equation/typographical errors in the gated aggregation description). These issues make the method harder to assess and reproduce.

The paper lacks detailed statistical validation for many central claims. Confidence intervals or significance tests are not consistently reported, and many reported gains overlap substantially across seeds, weakening the claim of consistent superiority.

The significance of the contribution is unclear relative to existing EEG foundation models. If discrete tokens are merely a different input representation but downstream performance is only sometimes improved, the practical advantage over strong continuous-tokenization baselines is not firmly established.

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: discrete tokenization for single-channel EEG, with a model-agnostic vocabulary of time-frequency motifs.

Proposes a technically sound dual-path architecture combining a Localized Spectral Window Encoder, temporal encoder, frequency/temporal transformers, and VQ codebook, with joint frequency-temporal masked prediction.
Extensive evaluation on four EEG benchmarks under single- and multi-dataset pretraining, showing consistent gains over strong baselines such as BIOT, LaBraM, EEGPT, and NeuroLM.
Demonstrates plug-and-play improvements when integrated into existing foundation models (BIOT, LaBraM), supporting the tokenizer's generality.
Includes a compelling cross-device scalability experiment on ear-EEG sleep staging, showing generalization beyond standard 10-20 montages.
Provides useful token-quality analyses (uniqueness, consistency, frequency learning, qualitative motif examples) and detailed appendix with hyperparameters and reproducibility information.
weaknesses: The core method combines existing ideas (VQ-VAE tokenization, masked modeling, dual time-frequency encoders) rather than introducing a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is mainly in the application and integration.
Some claims are stronger than the evidence: absolute class-token uniqueness scores remain low (e.g., 2.14% GM on TUEV), and the 'first' claims are difficult to fully verify.
The code/weights link appears missing in the manuscript, and there is an inconsistency in reported tokenizer parameter count (~0.7M in text vs. 1.2M in appendix).
Comparisons to LaBraM/BIOT rely on author-reproduced variants with limited pretraining rather than full-scale foundation models, which may affect how strongly the gains generalize.
Token codebook utilization is relatively low; while framed as compactness, it could indicate underutilized capacity or codebook collapse and deserves further investigation.

Qualitative motif analysis is small-scale and lacks systematic physiological validation; downstream-layer ablation suggests a 2-layer model may outperform the chosen 4-layer model on TUEV, raising hyperparameter-selection questions.
